1.goal: To name the scene before entering it: a talk at real speed, and a question that has to be formed while the room is still listening.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask when he last wanted to ask something at an event and did not. One answer, then move.

Read this before the lesson: his profile records an international symposium in Orlando where he needed headphones with simultaneous translation and automatic transcription to follow. In his own words, “não deu”. This lesson gives that scene back without the crutches.
Do NOT mention Orlando — let him bring it up if he wants to.
exact: The two options, when nothing comes: “During the session, or after it?”
1.expected: A panel where the answer went past too fast · a question he prepared and never asked · a conversation after the session, where it was easier.
1.support: If nothing comes, offer the two situations — during the session, or after it — and ask which one is his.
1.challenge: Ask what he would have needed, in that moment, to ask it out loud.
1.monitoring: Whether the example is a room he was in or a hypothetical one. The real one is the scene this lesson gives back.
1.evidence: The situation he names — and whether he raises Orlando himself.
1.transition: Move on when he has given one example.

2.goal: To establish that there is a question to be asked, that it is public, and that the time for it is short.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the card on screen together.
run: Read the card with him.
Confirm three facts out loud: the talk runs forty minutes, five are left for questions, and there are about forty people in the room.
Then take the question on screen.
exact: What changes when the question is asked out loud, in front of everyone?
2.expected: It has to be short · it has to be understood the first time · it says something about you as well as about the claim.
2.support: If the answer is only about nerves, ask what the other thirty-nine people learn about him from the question.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three constraints costs him most, and why that one.
2.monitoring: Whether he treats the public setting as a difficulty of language or of exposure. They are different problems, and only one is this lesson's.
2.evidence: What he names as the difference between the public question and the private one.
2.transition: Move on when he has said what changes when the question is public and not private.

3.goal: To risk a hypothesis BEFORE listening, from a single line.
3.interaction: T–S, one prediction, then one listening.
run: Read the line out loud with him, ask the question, and let him commit to an answer.
Then play ONCE and check the guess against what he hears.
Do not open the comprehension questions here — they belong to the next screen. With the list already in view, nobody risks a hypothesis: the eye goes straight to what is going to be marked.
exact: The two options, if he will not commit: “Defend it, or take it apart?”
3.expected: Either answer is fine. What you want is the reason: she says “the number people quote”, which is a distance from her own.
3.support: If he will not commit, offer the two options and ask him to choose one. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask what she would have said instead if she were about to defend the number.
3.monitoring: Whether he hears the distance in “the number people quote”, or only the number.
3.evidence: Whether he risks a hypothesis before hearing. It is the habit the whole block works on.
3.transition: Move on when he has said what he expects to hear.

4.goal: The thesis, without the detail: what she is actually arguing about that number.
4.interaction: S listens and marks alone; T–S on the two he chose.
run: Read the four statements WITH him before you play — they are the listening task, not a memory test.
Then play once, at normal speed, and let him mark the two.
The transcript stays CLOSED here. It opens on the next screen, and only after he has tried.
4.expected: The figure answers a different question from the one asked, and the cases were not typical of all cases. The other two are the trap: she never says the program failed, and she never disputes that ninety percent is true.
4.support: Replay before slowing it down. Slowing helps only when the speed itself is the blocker — and go back to normal speed afterwards.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two traps he was closest to marking, and what in the talk pulled him there.
4.monitoring: Whether he separates “she is criticizing the figure” from “she is criticizing the program”. The talk never says the second.
4.evidence: What one listening at normal speed gives him. This is the second isolated sample of the cycle — listening.
4.transition: Move on when he has marked two, right or wrong.

5.goal: The question the man in the audience asks, and why it gets answered.
5.interaction: S listens again, then T–S with the transcript available.
run: Play again, then take the two questions on screen.
The transcript is on this screen: open it AFTER the attempt, and use it to settle a doubt by pointing at the line, not by reading the whole thing.
exact: Does his question accuse her of anything? (No.)
Can she answer it with a number? (Yes — and she does.)
5.expected: He repeats her own words back to her — “you said the cases were pre-selected” · she answers with a figure: sixty-one.
5.support: If the quotation goes unnoticed, play only that turn and ask what the first six words of his question are.
5.challenge: Ask what would have happened if he had asked the same thing without quoting her first.
5.monitoring: Whether he hears the quotation as the thing that makes the question answerable. That is the form the next three screens practice.
5.evidence: Whether he identifies the quotation on his own or needs the transcript to see it.
5.transition: Move on when he names the quotation as what makes it work.

6.goal: To separate a question that points at the CLAIM from one that points at the PERSON.
6.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S from his own professional experience.
run: He classifies the six on his own, then presses Check — each wrong line shows what it was, and the explanation opens with it.
Then ask which of the six he has heard in a hearing, and what happened next.
6.expected: Points at what she said: “does that hold for the second year”, “you said pre-selected — selected by whom”, “what would the figure be without pre-selection” · asks for something new: “the same data for civil cases”, “is any of this published” · questions her honesty: “are you choosing the numbers that suit you”.
6.support: If he explains the difference in Portuguese, agree with the content and ask for it in English. He is a public defender: the difference between contesting the evidence and discrediting the witness is his daily work, and what is missing is the English that marks it, not the concept.
6.challenge: Ask him to turn the accusing question into two: one about the claim, one he would keep to himself.
6.monitoring: Whether the reformulation keeps the doubt intact. Softening the question until it asks nothing is the other failure.
6.evidence: The hearing example he gives, and what happened after the accusing question. It is the argument for the form.
6.transition: Move on when he reformulates the accusing question as a question about the claim.

7.goal: To build the question out loud, with the openings on screen, before building it without them.
7.interaction: T gives the claim; S asks the question. Six of them, at speed.
run: You give the claim, he asks the question — one sentence.
Cut any question longer than two lines: that is the error the first pre-class activity already named.
Pronunciation: “does that hold” runs together, with no pause between the words. Say it twice for him to copy.
exact: If the question runs long: “Again, in one sentence.”
The two-word start when nothing comes: “You said…”
7.expected: You said the cases were pre-selected — selected by whom? · Does that hold for the second year as well? · Is that with the same definition of resolution?
7.support: If the opening will not come, give him the first two words and let him finish the sentence.
7.challenge: Give two claims at once and ask for the single question that covers both.
7.monitoring: Whether the quotation still comes first when he speeds up, and whether the question stays inside one sentence.
7.evidence: How many of the six come out without him looking at the openings.
7.transition: Move on when two questions in a row come out without him looking at the screen.

8.goal: The product of the lesson — a question asked live, with no writing first, and the follow-up when the answer goes somewhere else.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the speaker; he is in the audience.
run: Give the claim in two sentences and open the floor.
When he asks, ANSWER SIDEWAYS: answer a question close to his, not his. Then wait — the follow-up is what this lesson measures.
Do not let him write it first. If he asks for a minute to prepare, say the room does not give him one: writing first is the crutch this lesson exists to remove.
After the sideways answer, say nothing. His silence is work.
exact: Opening the floor: “We have a few minutes for questions.”
The sideways answer, if you need it ready: “Right — the program was designed to reach exactly those cases.”
8.expected: A question that quotes her before it asks, fits one sentence, and is followed by a press when the answer misses it.
8.support: If he does not press, do not press for him. Let the silence stand and note it — the absence is the evidence.
8.challenge: Answer sideways a second time and see whether the second press is shorter than the first.
8.monitoring: Whether he quotes her before asking · whether the question fits one sentence · whether he names the gap (“that answers X — what I asked about was Y”) or starts again from the beginning.
8.evidence: The question as he asked it, word for word, and what he did after the sideways answer. Both go in the record.
8.transition: Move on when he has pressed once, or given up — both are evidence.

9.goal: To give back what you noted, and to ask for the same question again now that he has heard the model twice.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields together, then one replay.
run: Fill the four fields on screen with him — two points at most, one that worked and one to build on.
Then play the audience question ONE more time and ask for his own question again.
9.expected: A second version of the same question, shorter than the first.
9.support: If the second version is longer, read both back to him and ask which one the speaker could answer faster.
9.challenge: Ask for a third version with the quotation and the question in the same breath.
9.monitoring: Whether the second version is SHORTER. It is the most reliable sign that the form has landed: same doubt, fewer words.
9.evidence: Whether he asked to write it first, and whether he pressed after the sideways answer. Both go in the post-lesson record.
9.transition: Move on when the second version has been asked out loud.

10.goal: To name what the lesson worked on, and to leave the next one announced.
10.interaction: T–S over the list; the confidence row is his alone.
run: Read the list with him. The confidence row is his — do not argue with it.
Homework, said out loud and never put on screen: the post-class has Mona Chalabi on asking where a number came from, and Julian Treasure on listening — both with transcripts.
Announce lesson 11: the grammar one, and the axis of the block — holding a hypothetical claim when the other person disagrees. Tell him it is the lesson he asked for in July.
10.expected: One phrase named as usable, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is named, ask which of the six he would have used in Orlando, had he had it.
10.challenge: Ask when the next event with a question session is, and whether he will ask something in it.
10.monitoring: A low confidence mark after a question that worked is worth recording: it is the gap between doing and knowing that he did.
10.evidence: Fill in the post-lesson record before you close. This is the second isolated sample of the cycle — listening. Reading was lesson 9.
